---
title: Inflatables Report 10/4/2019
---

The design pipeline that we currently envision consists of the following steps:

1. Parametrization: flatten the target 3D surface to the plane with a mapping
   that stretches the surface by
   $\alpha_\text{min} \le \alpha \le \frac{\pi}{2}$
   along one direction and leaves the orthogonal direction unstretched. This is so that
   the *inverse mapping* from the plane to the target surface contracts lengths by $\frac{2}{\pi}$
   just like the air channel mechanism.
2. Trace air channel walls along the unstretched direction field with
   thickness determined by the value of $\alpha$ at each point.
3. Simulate the inflation of these air channels (and build atop this simulation
   an optimization of the wall curves to better fit the inflated structure to
   the target surface).

So far, I have been working primarily on stages 1 and 3, and this document
provides an update on my progress.

## Parametrization

### Formulation
We seek a mapping $f : \mathcal{M} \to \mathbb{R}^2$ of a target surface
$\mathcal{M} \subset \mathbb{R}^3$  to the plane that is "compatible" with the
air channel inflation mechanism. The most obvious requirement on $f$ can be expressed
in terms of the singular value decomposition of its Jacobian at each point
on the surface:
$$
    \nabla f = U
    \begin{pmatrix}
        \sigma_0 & 0 & 0 \\
        0 & \sigma_1 & 0
    \end{pmatrix}
    V^T,
\label{eqn:svd}\tag{1}
$$
where $U \in \mathbb{R}^{2 \times 2}$ is a matrix whose two columns give the
directions *in the plane* along which lengths are stretched or preserved
respectively, $\sigma_0$ and $\sigma_1$ are the stretching amounts along these directions,
and $V \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3}$ indicates the directions in 3D
space that are stretched by the mapping (we do not care so much about $V$).

To be compatible with the air channel mechanism, $f$ must have $\sigma_1 = 1$ and
$\sigma_0$ in some admissible stretching range $\left[\alpha_\text{min}, \frac{\pi}{2}\right]$.
Setting $\alpha_\text{min} = \frac{\pi}{2}$ would mean all air channels are of "full width,"
while choosing $\alpha_\text{min} \in \left(1, \frac{\pi}{2}\right)$ means the air channels
are allowed to be narrower than the air channel spacing (so a band of fused
material fits between each channel).
It appears that allowing $\alpha_\text{min} \lt \frac{\pi}{2}$ enables significantly more
flexibility in the space of surfaces that can be flattened.

Mappings of this form were already constructed in @aharoni, which ran an iterative
"local-global" optimization to fit $\nabla f$ to the desired form by minimizing the energy:
$$
E[f] :=
\min_{U, V, \alpha} \frac{1}{2} \int_\mathcal{M} \! \left\| \nabla f -
    U
    \begin{pmatrix}
        \alpha & 0 & 0 \\
        0 & 1 & 0
    \end{pmatrix}
    V^T
 \right\|_F^2 \ \mathrm{d}A.
\label{eqn:lgparam}\tag{2}
$$
Their approach alternates between (i) computing a closed-form solution to the
minimization over $U$, $V$ and $\alpha$ (found by computing the SVD of the current
Jacobian $\nabla f$ for each triangle and setting $\alpha$ to $\sigma_0$ clamped
to the admissible range); and (ii) solving for the optimal mapping $f$
while holding the newly computed $U$, $V$ and $\alpha$ fixed.
As long as this method is run from a reasonable initialization, it quickly
reaches a parametrization $f$ with singular values close to the admissible range (provided
such a mapping exists).

Unfortunately, as seen in the following figure, this approach results in noisy
"stretch factors" $\alpha$ and orientations that would be difficult to trace air
channels through:

![Figure 1: Result of local-global optimization $(\ref{eqn:lgparam})$ with $\alpha_\text{min} = 1.4$ on the Lilium tower surface.](images/LocalGlobalLiliumPlot.png)

Here, the orientations are visualized by taking the angle between the stretching direction and the plane's $x$ axis and
interpreting it is a hue in the HSV color space (actually, we visualize
twice this angle because rotating a stretching direction by $\pi$ gives the
same channel orientation).

To encourage more structure in the stretching factor and orientation fields, we need to add some regularization terms to $(\ref{eqn:lgparam})$.
After adding these terms, we will no longer be able to use the local-global optimization approach of solving for optimal $U, \alpha,$ and $V$ in closed form
(for fixed $f$). We instead must directly tackle the nonlinear optimization problem of minimizing the mapping energy:
$$
E[f] := \underbrace{\frac{1}{2} \int_\mathcal{M}
                    (\sigma_1 - 1)^2 + \left(\sigma_0 - \texttt{clamp}(\sigma_0, (\alpha_\text{min}, \pi / 2))\right)^2 \mathrm{d}A
        }_{\text{singular value fitting term}}
      + \underbrace{
            \frac{w_\phi}{p_\phi} \sum_{i, j} \sin(|\phi_i - \phi_j|)^{p_\phi}
        }_{\text{direction regularization}}
      + \underbrace{
            \frac{w_\alpha}{p_\alpha} \sum_{i, j} |\alpha_i  - \alpha_j|^{p_\alpha}
        }_{\text{stretch regularization}},
\label{eqn:rparam}\tag{3}
$$
where the sums in the regularization terms are over the mesh edges (indexed by adjacent triangles $i$ and $j$).
These regularization terms are expressed in terms of functions of (the SVD of) Jacobian $\nabla f$ on triangles $i$ and $j$:
we've defined $\alpha_i$ to be triangle $i$'s largest singular value ($\sigma_0$)
and $\phi_i$ to be the angle between the corresponding left singular vector
(i.e., the first column of $U$ in $(\ref{eqn:svd})$) and the $x$ axis.
The direction regularization term can also be written in the equivalent form:
$$
  \frac{w_\phi}{p_\phi} \sum_{i, j} \|{\bf u}_i \times {\bf u}_j\|^{p_\phi},
$$
where ${\bf u}_i$ and ${\bf u}_j$ are first left singular vectors for triangles $i$ and $j$.

Weights $w_\phi$ and $w_\alpha$ control the trade-off between preferring smoothness in the
corresponding fields and fitting to the admissible singular values. Parameters
$p_\phi$ and $p_\alpha$ control the type of smoothness/structure we ask for.
For instance, setting $p_\phi = 2$ requests that stretching orientations vary
smoothly across the surface, while $p_\phi = 1$ requests more of a
"zig-zagging" map with patches of nearly straight air channels that abruptly
change direction across a sparse network of seams.

The results shown here are for the "Lilium Tower" surface mesh, which has a mixture of
negative and positive curvature:

#### Local-Global Parametrization, $\alpha_\text{min} = 1.4$
The following results use $\alpha_\text{min} = 1.4$ (corresponding to a minimum channel width of ~70% of the channel spacing). The
result from the unregularized, local-global alternating minimization
$(\ref{eqn:lgparam})$ were already shown in Figure 1 above, but I repeat them here, this time
adding a quiver plot visualization of the orientations and a histogram of the
singular values:

[![](images/LocalGlobalLiliumPlot.png){width=800px}        ](images/LocalGlobalLiliumPlot.png){target=".blank"}
[![](images/lilium_local_global_quiver.png){width=400px}   ](images/lilium_local_global_quiver.png){target=".blank"}

(Click for larger images.)
As the histogram shows, the singular values mostly fit to their target values, though
we see a considerable number of triangles with singular values less than $1.4$ or
greater than $\frac{\pi}{2} \approx 1.508$. The min/max statistics for the
singular values are:

|            |   min   |   max  |
|------------|---------|--------|
| $\sigma_0$ | 1.3495  | 1.6045 |
| $\sigma_1$ | 0.9347  | 1.0523 |


#### Regularized Parametrization, $\alpha_\text{min} = 1.4$
Running the regularized parametrization $(\ref{eqn:rparam})$with
$p_\phi = p_\alpha = 2$ to prefer smooth fields and using weights $w_\alpha = 10^{-5}, w_\phi =
5\times 10^{-6}$ yields a much smoother orientation field and actually better
satisfaction of the stretching bounds:

## Inflation Simulation

On the simulation side, I have implemented the approach described in
[[@Skouras2014]](http://www-labs.iro.umontreal.ca/~bernhard/PDF/InflatableStructures.pdf),
which models the sheets as incompressible neo-Hookean membranes with no bending
stiffness. My implementation supports enabling and disabling the Tension-field Theory
approximation (where compressive forces are neglected to avoid the numerical
challenges involved in resolving local sheet buckling/crinkling).

When the pressure is high enough for the true equilibrium to have tension
almost everywhere, Tension-field Theory gives essentially identical results to
the full neo-Hookean simulation while converging significantly faster. For
lower pressures, Tension-field Theory can give weird results with highly
compressed/inverted regions (since compression is not penalized).

I have run a few experiments so far on some simple parametric designs to validate the simulation:

As expected, the sheets contract in the direction perpendicular to the channels, but then
somewhat surprisingly, they roll up (note: my simulation does not detect/avoid collisions).
This can be explained by the fact that the channel sidewalls prefer to contract into
mildly concave shapes, which is only possible if the channels
roll out of plane. I would be interested to see if this rolling effect is seen
in physical experiments--have you tried this experiment?

### Concentric Circles
<center>
<video height="400px" width="600px" loop playsinline controls>
    <source src="videos/hyperbolic_disk.mp4" type="video/mp4">
</video>
</center>

This experiment eventually worked as expected, although initially I was not setting a high
enough pressure, which caused the Tension-field based simulation to give
non-physical results. Is there a rule of thumb we can use for predicting the
inflation pressure needed?

You'll notice that after the structure appears to have fully inflated, the
saddle orientation still rotates for a while; during this stage, the simulation
is able to very slightly increase the volume.
My interpretation is that, even though the rotationally symmetric design
does not prefer any particular saddle orientation, my surface
triangulation does have a slight asymmetry which the simulation is exploiting:
<center>
![](images/concentric_circles_mesh.png){width=300px}
</center>
(The blue circles indicate the vertices at which the top and bottom sheets are fused
together.)

### Radial Channels

I also tried a design with straight radial walls, which I expected to contract
into a cone:
<center>
![](images/radial_channels_mesh.png){width=400px}
</center>

That is not quite what happened. Depending on the applied pressure, either the
sheet buckled in to a configuration with a crease at each wall density
transition or into a folded mess (that was at least closer to what I expected):
<a name="kinks"></a>
<center>
![](images/radial_channels_kinked_cone.png){width=400px}
![](images/radial_channels_crinkled_cone.png){width=300px}
</center>

I am wondering if a bending energy term is needed to avoid configurations like
the one on the left--or maybe this actually a valid equilibrium?
Could it be realized in practice?
